title: Endometrial Polyp
study_design: Educational review of the evaluation and management of endometrial polyps; no original research design is reported.
clinical_background: Endometrial polyps are localized growths of endometrial glands and stroma within the uterine cavity. They may occur alone or in multiples and range from a few millimeters to several centimeters. They can be diagnosed at any age, with peak incidence between 40 to 49 years old. Most are benign, although malignant transformation is possible. Patients may have no symptoms or present with abnormal uterine bleeding.
objectives: Review the evaluation and management of endometrial polyps.
Identify risk factors for developing an endometrial polyp.
Describe the usual clinical presentation of patients with endometrial polyps.
Describe typical imaging findings associated with endometrial polyps.
Explain how communication and collaboration within the interprofessional team support the selection of patients for surgical management and improve outcomes.
main_conclusion: Endometrial polyps are usually benign, but evaluation should account for abnormal bleeding and the possibility of malignancy. Observation is an option for asymptomatic, low-risk patients, while hysteroscopic polypectomy is the standard treatment when removal is appropriate; the polyp and surrounding endometrium should undergo histological assessment.
narrative_summary:
This clinical review describes the presentation, evaluation, and management of endometrial polyps rather than reporting an original study. Polyps occur across age groups, with peak incidence at 40 to 49 years. They may cause abnormal uterine bleeding or remain asymptomatic. Malignant transformation is reported in 0 to 13%; malignant polyps are reported in 4.47% of symptomatic postmenopausal females versus 1.51% of asymptomatic postmenopausal females. Chronic tamoxifen use is associated with endometrial abnormalities, including polyps, in 20% to 35% of females.

Transvaginal ultrasound may show endometrial thickening, while saline-infusion sonography (SIS) helps distinguish a polyp from a submucosal fibroid. Imaging cannot establish a tissue diagnosis. Because blind endometrial biopsy or dilation and curettage (D&C) is inaccurate for diagnosing polyps, the review says these approaches should be used only when hysteroscopic treatment is unavailable. Asymptomatic, low-risk patients may be observed with periodic ultrasound assessment; one cited trial found spontaneous resolution in 29% of premenopausal patients after 1 year. Hormonal treatment has insufficient support and cannot currently be recommended. Hysteroscopic polypectomy is the standard treatment, although its timing remains unclear in asymptomatic, low-risk patients. Histologically confirmed polyps recur at approximately 2.5% to 3.7%. Evidence on polyps and infertility is conflicting: a cited randomized trial found improved pregnancy rates after polypectomy before intrauterine insemination, whereas a cited retrospective IVF review found no difference in pregnancy, miscarriage, or live-birth rates.
interpretation: Most endometrial polyps are benign, but malignancy is possible and is related to factors including age, menopausal status and bleeding symptoms. Abnormal uterine bleeding is the most frequent symptom, although some patients have no symptoms. Hysteroscopic polypectomy can substantially improve intermenstrual bleeding, and recurrence of histologically confirmed polyps is approximately 2.5% to 3.7%. The relationship between polyps and infertility remains uncertain.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: A cited trial found spontaneous resolution after 1 year in 29% of premenopausal patients. Studies cited in the article report increased rates of spontaneous pregnancy and term delivery after hysteroscopic polypectomy, and a prospective randomized controlled trial found improved pregnancy rates when polypectomy preceded intrauterine insemination. In contrast, a retrospective review of patients with known polyps during IVF cycles found no difference in pregnancy, miscarriage or live-birth rates.
clinical_implications: Malignant polyps are more prevalent among symptomatic postmenopausal females than among asymptomatic postmenopausal females: 4.47% versus 1.51%. This risk makes tissue diagnosis relevant when evaluating a polyp.
Imaging can identify and characterize a suspected polyp but cannot establish its histological diagnosis. Neither polyp location, number nor diameter correlates with reported symptoms.
Polyps greater than 1.5 cm in length are less likely to resolve without treatment.
Hysterectomy eliminates polyp recurrence and the potential for malignancy, but entails significantly greater patient risk and cost.
The presence of polyps, and discussion of their possible malignancy, can affect quality of life and mental well-being.
practice_implications: For abnormal uterine bleeding, assess its cause, severity, associated symptoms and comorbidities; obtain a comprehensive medical, surgical and bleeding history, and examine the cervix and vaginal vault for other structural causes.
Consider a urine pregnancy test, complete blood count and coagulation panel when evaluating abnormal uterine bleeding to assess for anemia and coagulopathy.

Use transvaginal ultrasound for pelvic imaging. Saline-infusion sonography (SIS) can better delineate a polyp and distinguish it from a submucosal fibroid; avoid SIS in pregnancy or active uterine or cervical infection.

Consider tissue sampling because a polyp can contain malignancy. Histological diagnosis requires an endometrial biopsy, dilation and curettage (D&C), or hysteroscopic polypectomy; because blind biopsy and D&C are inaccurate for diagnosing polyps, use them only when hysteroscopic treatment is unavailable.
Observation with periodic ultrasound assessment is an option for asymptomatic, low-risk patients. Hormonal medical management has insufficient support and cannot currently be recommended.

Hysteroscopic polypectomy is the standard treatment. Submit the polyp and surrounding endometrium for histological evaluation, and consider polypectomy for symptomatic patients with polyps greater than 1.5 cm in length.
Contemplate hysterectomy only after extensive patient counseling about its greater risks and cost.
Consider daily iron supplementation when abnormal uterine bleeding has caused anemia.
If postoperative pathology identifies malignancy, refer the patient to gynecology oncology.

Recurrence rates are reported to decrease further when hysteroscopic polypectomy is combined with endometrial ablation or insertion of a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device, but supporting data are limited and their use for this purpose is currently restricted to research protocols. A levonorgestrel intrauterine device (IUD) may be considered for tamoxifen-associated polyps because it has been shown to reduce polyp formation.
The expert recommendation reported in the article is to remove endometrial polyps before in-vitro fertilization.

Counsel patients about abnormal uterine bleeding, the usually benign nature of polyps, possible malignancy, recurrence, quality of life and future fertility. Discuss procedural benefits, risks, alternatives and outcomes without using terminology that may cause unnecessary concern.

Evaluate abnormal uterine bleeding for more serious causes, including malignancy. For high-risk surgical patients, consider an anesthesia consultation; coordinate surgical preparation and postoperative follow-up through the healthcare team.
limitations: The literature provides limited support for hormonal medical management of endometrial polyps.
Data supporting endometrial ablation or intrauterine devices to reduce recurrence after polypectomy are limited.
Evidence concerning the relationship between endometrial polyps and infertility is conflicting.
open_questions: The definitive cause of endometrial polyps is unknown.
The appropriate timing of routine hysteroscopic polypectomy in asymptomatic, low-risk patients remains unclear.

document_sections.heading: Continuing Education Activity
document_sections.content: Endometrial polyps are proliferations of endometrial glands and stroma within the uterine cavity. Their diameter ranges from a few millimeters to several centimeters. They may occur singly or as multiple growths occupying the entire cavity. This activity addresses their assessment and management and the interprofessional team's role in caring for affected patients.

document_sections.heading: Objectives:
document_sections.content: The learning objectives are to identify risk factors for endometrial polyps, describe their usual clinical presentation and imaging findings, and explain how interprofessional communication and collaboration support appropriate selection for surgery and better outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Endometrial polyps consist of excess endometrial glands and stroma within the uterine cavity. They range from a few millimeters to several centimeters in diameter and may be solitary or numerous enough to occupy the entire cavity. They can be diagnosed at any age, but incidence peaks between the age of 40 to 49 years old. They are regarded as benign, although a small risk of malignant transformation remains.

document_sections.heading: Etiology
document_sections.content: These polyps are localized proliferations of endometrial glands and stroma that project from the endometrium. Their definitive cause is unknown. Because they are associated with endometrial hyperplasia, unopposed estrogen is considered a risk factor. Other factors linked to their development include increased endometrial aromatase activity, TGF-beta, VEGF, BCL-2, and genetic factors. Endometrial abnormalities, including polyps, occur in 20% to 35% of females receiving chronic tamoxifen therapy. Most polyps are benign, but malignant transformation can occur in 0 to 13%. Malignancy within a polyp is related to age and menopausal status: malignant polyps have a prevalence of 4.47% in symptomatic postmenopausal females versus 1.51% in asymptomatic postmenopausal females. Additional risk factors are age greater than 60, large-sized polyps, menopause status, symptomatic bleeding, and polycystic ovarian syndrome.

document_sections.heading: Epidemiology
document_sections.content: Endometrial polyps occur across all ages, with peak incidence between the age of 40 to 49. Among reproductive-aged women with abnormal uterine bleeding, estimated prevalence is between 20 to 40 percent. They are identified in approximately 10 percent of women at autopsy. Malignant polyps are less likely in premenopausal than in postmenopausal females.

document_sections.heading: Histopathology
document_sections.content: Endometrial polyps are epithelial proliferations containing vascular, glandular, fibromuscular, and connective tissues. Surface epithelium covers a predominantly vascular core. They may be sessile, pedunculated, or prolapsing. A prolapsed polyp can show squamous metaplasia, infection, or ulceration. In most polyps, the constituent endometrium differs from adjacent endometrium and does not react to cyclical hormonal changes. Other possible histological findings are carcinomatous, atrophic, or hyperplastic changes.

document_sections.heading: History and Physical
document_sections.content: Patients may have no symptoms; when symptoms occur, abnormal uterine bleeding is the most common. Abdominal pain, pelvic pain, and infertility may also occur. One in four reproductive-aged women with abnormal bleeding has an endometrial polyp in the cavity. Evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding should establish its cause and severity, associated symptoms, and comorbidities. A thorough medical and surgical history helps exclude other causes. No bleeding pattern is diagnostic of a polyp, but the bleeding history should be characterized; menorrhagia and intermenstrual spotting are reported most often. Tamoxifen, commonly used for breast cancer, can act as an agonist or antagonist in tissues bearing estrogen receptors. It has anticancer effects in breast tissue but carcinogenic effects in endometrial tissue. Chronic tamoxifen use is associated with endometrial polyps at an incidence of 20% to 35%. Hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms may also be associated with polyp formation, irregular bleeding, and ultrasound evidence of endometrial thickening. Clinical examination should include a general assessment, bimanual examination, and sterile speculum examination. The cervix and vaginal vault should be examined completely to exclude other structural explanations for symptoms. A pedunculated polyp may be visible at the external os.

document_sections.heading: Evaluation
document_sections.content: Transvaginal ultrasound is the most commonly used efficient imaging method for pelvic structures. Its findings may be nonspecific, with diffuse or focal echogenic thickening of the endometrium. In patients with postmenopausal bleeding, endometrial thickness of less than 4 mm is associated with atrophy, whereas thickness greater than 4 mm is associated with endometrial pathology, including polyps. Polyp location, number, and diameter do not correlate with reported symptoms. Saline-infusion sonography (SIS) assesses the uterine cavity by introducing about 5 to 30 mL of warmed saline through a thin catheter during the proliferative phase of the menstrual cycle. Fluid surrounding a mass improves visualization of polyps. Active uterine or cervical infection and pregnancy are contraindications. Compared with transvaginal ultrasound, SIS allows better evaluation of the adnexa and cornua and better distinction between submucosal fibroids and polyps: polyps arise from the endometrial layer, whereas submucosal fibroids are seen beneath it. Other assessment methods include hysterosalpingograms and hysteroscopy. The imaging methods do not establish a tissue diagnosis. Because polyps carry a malignancy risk, tissue sampling should be considered; options to obtain a tissue diagnosis are endometrial biopsy, dilation, and curettage (D&C), or hysteroscopic polypectomy. Blind sampling by biopsy or D&C is inaccurate for diagnosing polyps and should be reserved for settings without hysteroscopic treatment. Laboratory evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding should include a urine pregnancy test, complete blood count, and coagulation panel to assess for anemia and coagulopathy.

document_sections.heading: Treatment / Management
document_sections.content: Observation is an option for asymptomatic patients at low risk. Incidentally detected polyps can regress without treatment; one trial found spontaneous resolution of 29% of polyps after 1 year in premenopausal patients. Conservative care includes periodic ultrasound assessment of polyp growth. Evidence supporting hormonal medical treatment is limited, so it cannot currently be recommended. Hysteroscopic polypectomy is considered standard treatment. Because a polyp may coexist with endometrial disease, histological assessment should include both the polyp and surrounding endometrium. Benign polyps have been identified in 20% of cases diagnosed with endometrial carcinoma. The appropriate timing of hysteroscopic polypectomy in asymptomatic, low-risk patients remains uncertain. A retrospective study investigating timing found no malignancies in histological specimens and concluded that the timing of routine polypectomy in asymptomatic females was unclear. Polyps greater than 1.5 cm in length are less likely to regress spontaneously; polypectomy could be considered for symptomatic patients. Hysterectomy eliminates polyp recurrence risk and the potential for malignancy, but entails significantly greater patient risk and cost; it should be considered only after extensive counseling. Daily iron supplementation should be considered when abnormal uterine bleeding causes anemia.

document_sections.heading: Differential Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Conditions to distinguish from endometrial polyps include submucosal leiomyoma, adenomyoma, retained products of conception, endometrial hyperplasia, endometrial carcinoma, and uterine sarcomas.

document_sections.heading: Prognosis
document_sections.content: Significant improvement in intermenstrual bleeding has been reported after hysteroscopic polypectomy. Treatment is effective, with low recurrence among patients who initially had fewer polyps. For histologically confirmed polyps, recurrence is approximately 2.5% to 3.7%. Combining hysteroscopic polypectomy with endometrial ablation or insertion of a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device further reduces recurrence, but supporting data are limited and these approaches are currently confined to research protocols. For tamoxifen-associated polyps, a levonorgestrel intrauterine device (IUD) has been shown to reduce polyp formation and may be considered in management. Some studies reported increased rates of spontaneous pregnancy and delivery at term after hysteroscopic polypectomy. Fertility rates did not differ statistically between patients with polyps less than or equal to 1 cm and those with polyps greater than 1 cm or multiple polyps. First-trimester spontaneous abortion rates likewise showed no statistical difference between patients with small polyps and those with larger or multiple polyps.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: Specimens obtained during hysteroscopic polypectomy should undergo pathological examination. If follow-up pathology identifies malignancy in a polyp, referral to gynecology oncology is recommended for further care. Hysteroscopic polypectomy rarely causes complications, and intrauterine adhesion risk is low. Evidence regarding the relationship between endometrial polyps and infertility is conflicting. A prospective, randomized controlled trial found that polypectomy before intrauterine insemination improved pregnancy rates. Another study found significantly higher polyp prevalence among infertile patients with Fallopian tube obstruction than among those with patent tubes. By contrast, a retrospective review of patients with known polyps during in vitro fertilization (IVF) cycles found no difference in pregnancy, miscarriage, or live birth rates. The current expert recommendation is to remove polyps before in-vitro fertilization.

document_sections.heading: Deterrence and Patient Education
document_sections.content: Patient education should address the causes and management of abnormal uterine bleeding. Although most polyps are benign, counseling should also cover their potential for malignancy; discussing that possibility can adversely affect mental well-being. Polyps can affect quality of life and future fertility. Patients should be informed about recurrence and modifiable factors that may lower its risk.

document_sections.heading: Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
document_sections.content: Limited understanding of endometrial polyps can adversely affect patients' quality of life and mental health. Counseling about the condition should account for the excessive worry that terms such as “lesion” or “neoplasm” may provoke. Abnormal uterine bleeding warrants full assessment to exclude more serious causes, including malignancy. Low-risk patients may receive conservative management, while surgery is another option. Recurrence risk should be discussed; suitable patients may benefit from endometrial ablation and levonorgestrel intrauterine devices to lower that risk. When surgery is planned, an anesthesia consultation should be considered for high-risk patients. Specialized surgical nurses prepare patients before and after the procedure, manage intraoperative positioning, and arrange necessary supplies. Nursing staff can assess postoperative treatment success and relay concerns to the care team. All healthcare professionals should counsel patients about procedural benefits, risks, alternatives, and outcomes. Team communication and collaboration are emphasized to provide safe, patient-centered care.
